title: De Orthographia
author: Cassiodorus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1189.tmp1189.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Ad hujus similitudinem soni nostri conjunctas vocales digammon appellare voluerunt, ut est votum, virgo. Itaque in prima syl- laba digamma et vocalem oportuit poni, fotum, fir- go : quod et AEoli fecerunt et antiqui nostri, sicut scriptura in quibusdam libellis declarat. Hanc litte- ram Terentius Varro dum vult demonstrare, ita per- scribit VA : qui ergo in hac syllaba sonus est, idem litterae erit. Nos hodie u litteram in duarum potesta- tem coegimus; nam modo pro digamma scribitur, modo pro vocali.
passages.english: On the likeness of this sound, they wanted to call our conjoined vowels a digamma, as in votum, virgo. And so in the first syllable a digamma and a vowel ought to have been put, fotum, firgo: which both the Aeolians did and our ancients, as the writing in certain little books shows. Terentius Varro, wishing to demonstrate this letter, writes it out thus: VA. So whatever sound is in this syllable, the same will be that of the letter. We today have forced the letter u into the value of two [letters]; for it is written now for the digamma, now for the vowel.
passages.notes: The Latin of the first sentence is compressed; the sense seems to be that consonantal u before a vowel was regarded as a digamma. 'VA' is uncertain as transmitted; Varro's illustration may be corrupt.

passages.original: Lacrumae, an lacrimae; maxumus an maximus; et si quae similia sunt, quomodo scribi debeant, quae- situm est. Terentius Varro tradit Caesarem per i ejusmodi verba solitum esse enuntiare et scribere : inde propter auctoritatem tanti viri consuetudinem factam; sed ego in antiquiorum multo libris, quam Caius Caesar est, per u pleraque scripta invenio.
passages.english: Lacrumae or lacrimae; maxumus or maximus; and whatever similar [words] there are: it has been asked how they ought to be written. Terentius Varro reports that Caesar was accustomed to pronounce and write words of this kind with i, and that from this, because of the authority of so great a man, the usage was established; but I find most [of them] written with u in the books of men much older than Gaius Caesar.

passages.original: Intervallum duas ll habet; vallum enim ipsum non aliter scribitur, a quo intervallum. Varro dicit inter- valla esse spatia quae sint inter capita vallorum, id est stipidum, quibus vallum fit, unde caetera quoque spatia dicunt.
passages.english: Intervallum has two l's; for vallum itself, from which intervallum [comes], is written no other way. Varro says that intervalla are the spaces which are between the heads of the valli, that is, of the stakes of which a palisade is made; from which they also call other spaces [by this name].

passages.original: Itaque et ante, et post, si h littera cuicunque tali adjungatur, non sonabit. Haec enim natura voca- lium est, ut sive ante se, sive post se habeant h, quoquo genere, enuntiationem non impediant. Prae- terea in libro quem de Grammatica Varro scripsit, cum de litteris dissereret, ita k inter litteras non esse disputavit. Quod multo minus mirum, quam quod x quoque litteram esse negat. In quo quid vi- derit, nondum deprehendi : ipsius verba subjiciam. Litterarum partim sunt et dicuntur : ut, a et b; par- tim dicuntur et non sunt, ut h et x; partim sunt, neque dicuntur, ut p, ψ. Vehemens et vemens apud antiquos, et apud Ciceronem lego; aeque prehendo, et prendo, hercule et hercle, nihil et nil. Haec ob- servari eatenus poterunt consuetudine potius quam ratione, in his praecipue verbis quae aspirationem habere debent.
passages.english: And so, whether before or after, if the letter h is joined to any such [vowel], it will not sound. For this is the nature of vowels, that whether they have h before them or after them, in whatever way, it does not hinder the pronunciation. Moreover, in the book which Varro wrote On Grammar, when he was discussing letters, he argued thus that k is not among the letters. This is much less surprising than that he denies that x too is a letter. What he saw in this I have not yet grasped: I will append his own words. 'Of the letters, some both are and are called [letters], as a and b; some are called [so] and are not, as h and x; some are, and are not called [so], as p, ψ.' I read vehemens and vemens among the ancients and in Cicero; likewise prehendo and prendo, hercule and hercle, nihil and nil. These can be observed to that extent by usage rather than by rule, especially in those words which ought to have aspiration.
passages.notes: The list 'p, ψ' in Varro's quotation looks corrupt (perhaps originally Greek letters such as ψ and another); the sense is unclear.

passages.original: Narare per unum r scribitur, ut Varroni placet, secutus est enim etymologiam nominis ejus, qua gnarus dicitur quis, qui scit et accepit quod loqui debeat. Denique compositio verbi ita scribitur, igno- rare, quod non per duo r, sed per unum scribitur.
passages.english: Narare is written with one r, as Varro holds; for he followed the etymology of the word, by which someone is called gnarus who knows and has learned what he ought to say. Finally, the compound of the word is written thus, ignorare, which is written not with two r's but with one.

passages.original: Coqui, Gratus artigraphus per c primam syllabam, secundam per q scribendam putavit; non enim dici- mus cocere, sed coquere; ut Virgilius,
passages.english: Coqui ["to be cooked"]: Gratus the grammarian thought it should be written with c in the first syllable and with q in the second; for we do not say cocere but coquere; as Virgil [says],
passages.notes: "Gratus artigraphus" is an unidentified grammarian. The passage breaks off before the Virgil quotation.

passages.original: ideo ne non fores, sed ineffabile voces de- nuntiet. Nam si per b mutam enuntias, Ουράς, ή τόν πυλώνα άργίΟυρον, significabit, per u digammon ultima scilicet syllaba, de qua et nunc loquimur, scribetur. Tavellas significat. Persius : Balva de nare locutus; si vero haec, id est l, non praefulgeat littera, et una vo- calis natura longa non erit penultima, b muta decen- ter in scriptura tenebit locum : ita tamen, si non a masculino genere nomina fuerint figurata;
passages.english: so that it may not signify fores [doors], but convey an unspeakable word. For if you pronounce it with the mute b, it will signify οὐρὰς ἢ τὸν πυλῶνα ["tail or gateway"?]; with u as digamma, that is, in the last syllable, of which we are now speaking, it will be written. It signifies tavellas. Persius: "having spoken through a stammering nose" (balba de nare locutus). But if this letter, that is l, does not stand before it, and there is no vowel long by nature in the penultimate, the mute b will properly hold its place in writing; provided, however, that the nouns have not been formed from the masculine gender;
passages.notes: The text is badly corrupt. The point seems to be that balvas/valvas (folding doors) must be distinguished from balbas (stammering women), but the logic cannot be securely recovered. The Greek "Ουράς, ή τόν πυλώνα άργίΟυρον" is garbled; I have rendered it only tentatively. "Tavellas" is unclear (possibly tabellas, "tablets"). The Persius quotation is usually read "balba de nare locutus"; the text has "Balva".

passages.original: ut Lucii, magnii, magii : quod ipsium Luci- lius adnotavit, eum a numero numerius discerneret. Cum praepositio, per c scribenda est : quum adver- bium temporis, quod significat quando, per q scri- bendum est, discretionis causa; ut apud Ennium,
passages.english: as Lucii, Magnii, Magii: which very thing Lucilius noted, when he distinguished numerius from numerus. Cum, the preposition, is to be written with c; quum, the adverb of time which means 'when', is to be written with q, for the sake of distinction; as in Ennius,
passages.notes: 'ipsium' read as 'ipsum'; 'eum' read as 'cum'. The passage breaks off before the Ennius quotation.

passages.original: Notandum igitur quod hamus, qui a Graecis ar/xwrrcw appellatur, cum aspiratione debet scribi. Sciendum et hoc pro ψ Graeco, a Latinis in scribendo ph poui debere, in Graecis duntaxat nominibus, ut, Orpheus, Phaeton. In caeteris autem Latinis nominibus f po- nendum, ut, fama, filius, facies. Phoebus, quo no- mine Apollo significatur, ita ponendum est, ut post p, h ponatur. Similiter et Herichthonius [ms., Hieri- cthonis], hiulcus, per aspirationem debent scribi.
passages.english: It should be noted, then, that hamus [hook], which the Greeks call ἄγκιστρον, ought to be written with aspiration. This too should be known: in place of Greek φ the Latins ought to put ph in writing, but only in Greek names, such as Orpheus, Phaethon. In other, Latin names, however, f should be put, as in fama, filius, facies. Phoebus, the name by which Apollo is signified, should be written so that h is placed after p. Likewise Herichthonius [manuscript: Hiericthonis] and hiulcus [gaping] ought to be written with aspiration.
passages.notes: "ar/xwrrcw" is a scanning error, read as ἄγκιστρον (hook). The printed ψ should be φ, and "poui" should be poni. "Herichthonius" is evidently Erichthonius.
